statement: Open question, still unmeasured. Verified premises: Playground §VI says 'just-in-time (JIT) compilation can be slow (1-3 minutes on Playground's tasks)'; the Newton tutorial says 'the first run compiles CUDA kernels, this can take a minute' and that 'the first step of any simulation is always the slowest'. Partial answer from the MuJoCo Warp documentation: kernels are compiled at first launch and cached on disk (~/.cache/warp), ahead-of-time compilation is supported, and compile time depends on the number of unique colliders that use the general convex pipeline, so the kernel set depends on model content. A model edit needs a host mj_compile ('1 call per new field instance'), put_model and a new graph capture; per-world parameter values are batched model fields and need no recompilation. Playground's own wall-clock curves show a compile region of roughly 20 to 75 s. No edit-to-first-step latency is published for any incumbent, so the 2-minute compile row used in C006 is not established for the Warp stack.

statement: With equal agent latency of 60 to 120 s per turn and about 300 s of incumbent training, a loop that evaluates one design per turn is capped at 3.5 to 6x per turn even if FrankenRobotics' compute time falls to zero. Reaching tenfold wall-clock on quadruped-class briefs therefore needs at least one more multiplicative factor.
